title: Civic Resilience and Democratic Defence Foundations
description: A nonpartisan, evidence-based introduction to public preparedness, lawful democratic defence, critical-service resilience, responsible cyber hygiene, emergency coordination, and competing models of national service. This is a civic learning course, not military recruitment, weapons, or combat training. Learners compare proposals—including universal two-year active service—using explicit evidence, rights, readiness, equity, workforce, and cost criteria.
creator: community-curation-draft
learning_outcomes: Distinguish the responsibilities and legal boundaries of military defence, civil protection, disaster management, law enforcement, and ordinary public services.
Explain constitutional civilian oversight, nonpartisanship, rights, accountability, and the principle that unlawful orders must not be obeyed.
Create an accessible household or community preparedness plan using reliable public guidance and lawful local emergency channels.
Identify when to seek accredited first-aid instruction and demonstrate only those practical skills assessed by a qualified instructor.
Describe basic cyber-hygiene practices and report a simulated incident while preserving provenance, privacy, and uncertainty.
Map dependencies in a fictional essential service and propose a recovery plan that respects resource limits and minimum service needs.
Compare voluntary military service, reserves, professional specialist careers, civil protection, civilian service, and universal-service proposals using a balanced and documented framework.
Draft a nonpartisan doctrine-and-learning charter that defines mission, authority, safeguards, readiness measures, independent review, and correction of mistakes.

syllabus.title: What public defence and resilience are for
topics: Public security as a public good
Military defence, civil protection, disaster management, and law enforcement: distinct mandates
Hazards, infrastructure disruption, cyber incidents, misinformation, and uncertainty
What a preparedness course can and cannot teach

syllabus.title: Constitution, law, rights, and civilian oversight
topics: Constitutional purposes and legal limits of defence institutions
Civilian authority, parliamentary oversight, and nonpartisanship
International humanitarian law and human-rights foundations
Duty to question and refuse manifestly unlawful orders
Conscientious objection, accessibility, appeal, and due process

syllabus.title: Personal and community preparedness
topics: Household communication and check-in plans
Accessible emergency planning and support for people with disabilities or care responsibilities
Recognizing emergencies and using official reporting channels
Evacuation readiness, shelter information, and community mutual aid
Preparedness limits and avoiding false confidence

syllabus.title: First aid and safe emergency support
topics: Scene safety and when to call emergency services
First-aid and CPR learning pathways delivered by qualified instructors
Fire, heat, flood, and environmental-hazard awareness
Responder role limits, consent, safeguarding, and handover
Practical assessment must be conducted by an appropriately qualified instructor

syllabus.title: Cyber hygiene, evidence, and trustworthy reporting
topics: Account security, updates, backups, and phishing awareness
Safe reporting of a simulated cyber incident
Distinguishing observation, assertion, inference, verification, and unknown
Privacy, least privilege, and avoiding unauthorized investigation
Why a digital signature does not by itself prove a claim is true

syllabus.title: Critical infrastructure and service continuity
topics: Electricity, water, telecommunications, transport, healthcare, and supply dependencies
Single points of failure and common-cause disruptions
Minimum service levels, scarce resources, and feasible recovery plans
Coordination across organizations without erasing local authority
Synthetic tabletop exercise: a fictional town loses power and communications

syllabus.title: Service models and better defence institutions
topics: South Africa's existing South African National Service Institute (SANSI) youth-service/learnership initiative and the public 30-year force-planning process as subjects for critical study, not parallel Praxis programmes
Voluntary professional forces, reserve models, conscription, and civilian service
Comparing universal two-year active service with shorter, modular, and role-specific alternatives
Recruitment, training capacity, instructor quality, retention, and total lifecycle cost
Specialist roles in medicine, cyber defence, logistics, engineering, communications, and civil protection
Doctrine as a versioned, evidence-reviewed public-interest framework
Independent after-action learning, safety reporting, and institutional accountability

syllabus.title: Capstone: design and evaluate a resilience pathway
topics: Map a fictional community's essential services and dependencies
Build an evidence-bounded recovery plan under a fixed resource budget
Identify authority, privacy, accessibility, and legal constraints
Compare service-policy alternatives using a transparent rubric
Present a nonpartisan learning plan and identify open questions
Use benchmark fixture PRAXIS-NRES-002-FIXTURE-001 to compare service models under explicit synthetic constraints; report uncertainty and hard-fail conditions
Structured capstone workbook with evidence ledger, resource-feasibility checks, and conditional policy recommendation

metadata.assessment_principle: criterion-referenced reasoning; no political-affiliation or enlistment-propensity scoring
